newsitem.title: USA: MindSpring bucks trend to court $19.95 customers.
newsitem.headline: MindSpring bucks trend to court $19.95 customers.

text.p: Mike McQuary has a message for the Internet service providers dumping individual Internet users and $19.95 a month flat-fee pricing to chase after business customers -- they're wimps.

McQuary, 36, is the contrarian-minded president and chief operating officer of MindSpring Enterprises Inc., an Atlanta Internet service provider wooing home Internet users at a time when most of its competitors are fleeing the business, scared off by giants such as AT&T and MCI.

The risks of pursuing an Internet-on-the-cheap strategy are many. America Online's travails after instituting $19.95 a month pricing in December are well chronicled. Aggressive smaller players such as MindSpring and Earthlink Network Inc. have yet to show a profit for their efforts.
But that's not stopping McQuary, who talked about the company and the industry during a recent stopover in Los Angeles for the Spring Internet World convention.

Since 1995, MindSpring has grown from a local company serving 1,000 customers in the southeastern United States to one of the largest independent providers of residential dial-up Internet access in the country, with more than 280 local phone numbers in 50 states.
As of Dec. 31, MindSpring had 122,000 customers, 99 percent of whom are residential or home-based business users.

MindSpring bought its way to national prominence. After raising close to $36 million in two 1996 stock offerings, the company scooped up 8 Internet service providers, and the dial-up customers cast aside when PSINet and Nando.net shifted focus to higher-margin business customers. Since January, MindSpring has acquired three more service providers.

According to McQuary, Internet providers can keep customers happy and make money if they're doing what they should. That means not skimping on modems, phone lines and other network infrastructure, adding ISDN and 56 kilobits per second modem technology, but only when it's ready, and being honest when things go wrong.

Mindspring Chairman Charles Brewer, 37, a Stanford MBA who started the company three years ago, regularly reports on the company's foul-ups and steps being taken to rectify them in open letters to customers posted on the MindSpring Web site (http://www.mindspring.com/).

At MindSpring, doing the right thing also means offering a $19.95 a month flat rate along with other pricing options for customers who want to spend less or more. MindSpring customers choose from four price plans, starting with $6.95 a month for five hours and increasing to $26.95 for unlimited access and up to 10 megabytes of space for a personal Web page.

By the end of March, Mindspring will begin offering a suite of Windows 95 utilities from TuneUp.com (http://www.tuneup.com/) that automatically diagnose and fix problems on their computer's hard drive, update printer drivers and protect their PCs from viruses.
Internet providers will succeed only if the people who run them are in it for the long haul, McQuary said.

"I've been at the company about two years. And six weeks after I joined someone asked me what my exit strategy was," McQuary said. "I told them it was to retire at 55. They were astounded. There aren't too many (Internet service providers) in it for the long term. They get into the business to get rich, or get big and get bought out."

MindSpring's attention to customer service has had some tangible effects. Churn, the amount of customers who leave every month, is a comparatively low 3 percent. NetGuide recently gave MindSpring its People's Choice Award for best Internet service provider, and the company was graded a "B+" in a February 1997 Internet service provider round up in PC World magazine.

So far, MindSpring's acquisitions and swelling customer rolls haven't done much for the company's balance sheet, which remains in the red. For the year ended Dec. 31, the company reported a $7.6 million loss on $18.1 million in revenues, compared with a $2 million loss on revenues of $2.3 million in 1995. On March 18, MindSpring closed at $7.50 a share on Nasdaq, off its 52-week high of $13 but not far from its opening price of $8.

According to McQuary, however, the company's customer-conscious formula is working. In the last quarter of 1996, sales and marketing costs fell to 16 percent of revenue from 40 percent in the second quarter, and other business costs are dropping. At the rate things are going, the company should break even by the second quarter of the year and show a profit by the end of 1997, he said.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
